sections.synopsis: Another frontal system will bring a return of rain and windy conditions later today into Sunday. A trend toward drier and cooler conditions is expected toward the middle portion of next week as the storm track shifts south of Western Washington.
sections.short_term:
An upper trough axis is moving onshore over Western Washington early this morning as another, more vigorous system approaches the region just offshore. A combination of high tide and low atmospheric pressure will bring a renewed threat of minor coastal flooding to the San Juans and Western Whatcom county this morning. Seas in excess of 20 feet continue along coast beaches. Rain and wind will increase along the coast later this afternoon with rain spreading inland this evening into the overnight hours. Windy conditions will also develop tonight near the east entrance to the strait and adjacent areas with some gusts of 45-55 mph.

The front will shift east of the Cascades by early Sunday afternoon with winds gradually easing and post-frontal showers across the area. A cooler air mass will follow the front...so there will be enough instability for isolated thunderstorms...especially near the coast. Snow levels will fall to around 4000 feet Sunday night, but QPF will be light by this time for just light accumulation at some of the higher passes. An upper level trough will remain over the area on Monday for scattered showers mainly coast and higher terrain and high temperatures back to around seasonal levels.
sections.long_term: Drier conditions return to the area Monday night into Tuesday as the upper trough shifts eastward. Model solutions are falling into better agreement regarding the midweek system taking a further southward track and just brushing the southern portion of the CWA with some light precip on Wednesday. Ensembles favor cool and generally dry conditions to finish off next week with the potential for more active conditions returning thereafter.
sections.marine:
Numerous headlines remain in place as we're currently in between systems. SCA advisories are in effect this morning but as the day progresses, strong winds are slated to become more widespread as Gales become common across interior waters (minus Puget Sound but a SCA at the least may be needed) and Storm Force winds arrive for all of the coastal waters. The culprit is a sub 965 mb surface low swinging a cold front across the region this evening into the night hours. Along with winds, high seas are forecast around 20 ft today with a dominant period of 17 to 18 seconds, highly energetic. Seas will gradually decrease to 15 to 20 ft by Sunday morning. An additional increase to 20 to 25 appears likely in the afternoon. South winds will ease a bit on Sunday, but remain elevated especially for the Coastal Waters.

Winds subside further Monday into early Tuesday before increasing again going into midweek with a stronger weather system moving southwards well offshore. Confidence is leading towards developing high pressure for next weekend as benign conditions appear to be on the horizon.

sections.synopsis: A weakening high pressure ridge north of the Hawaiian Islands will keep trade wind speeds on the decreasing trend lasting into Saturday, then ridge and wind speeds strengthen from Saturday afternoon into early next week. Passing showers are possible over windward and mountain areas during this time period, mainly during the overnight to early morning hours. The next best chance for statewide rainfall may develop from Monday into Tuesday of next week, as the cloud remnants from an old cold front drift across the islands on the trade winds.
sections.short_term: Isolated showers are ongoing across windward areas of the island chain this evening. Coverage is expected to increase again overnight. The forecast remains on track with no updates needed at this time.
sections.prev_discussion:
Issued at 342 PM HST Fri Nov 13 2026 Radar shows isolated trade showers moving into most windward areas this afternoon. A few are still making it over to leeward areas, but rainfall amounts have been very light (just a few hundredths of an inch). Winds were averaging 10 to 20 mph, and the normal windy locations were gusting near 30 mph.

Weak upper level ridging will remain in place near Hawaii through the weekend. At the surface, a high pressure system will move from our northwest to our northeast. Monday, an upper level low will approach from the northwest. At the same time, but unrelated, a band of moisture associated with an old frontal boundary will move across the state from the northeast. This should lead to a brief increase in showers, but no significant rainfall is forecast. The best guess on timing for this band, according to the latest guidance, is Monday evening.

The upper level low will continue to weaken as it moves very close to Hawaii Wednesday into Thursday. With minimal cold air aloft, it is expected to result in a slight increase in instability, perhaps leading to a slight increase in both the coverage and intensity of showers. A new ridge aloft is forecast to move in from the west late next week. Throughout the entire period, trades will continue.
sections.marine:
A high pressure system north of Hawaii will slowly weaken through Saturday, allowing trade winds to slightly decrease tonight. A Small Craft Advisory (SCA) remains in effect for the typical windy waters near Maui County and the Big Island. By Saturday evening, a new high pressure will build north of the islands and restrengthen trade winds, likely leading to an expansion of the SCA to include additional waters. Next week will likely see continuing fresh to strong trades with some minor fluctuations each day. A moderate to large north-northwest swell is also expected to fill in early Sunday morning and elevate seas above 10 feet for coastal waters.

A moderate, north-northwest swell will continue to decline tonight into the weekend, allowing surf to become moderate to small and then small. A new small, north-northwest swell will support continued small surf into Saturday before the arrival of a more significant north swell. This moderate, long-period north swell arriving Saturday night may bring surf to advisory levels on Sunday for north and west- facing shores. Surf to at least moderate levels will last into Monday before the swell really begins to fade on Tuesday. A small to moderate northwest swell is then possible by next weekend.

Surf along east-facing shores will decrease slightly tonight and Saturday as trades ease early this weekend. Surf will increase again Sunday into early next week as trades restrengthen. South shore surf will stay tiny to small for the next few days, then a small, long-period swell could boost surf heights towards the end of next week.
